source: Gentner (1983) Structure-mapping: a theoretical framework for analogy, Cognitive Science 7:155-170
finding: Founding statement. An analogy maps relations between objects from base to target and drops object attributes. Which relations carry over is set by systematicity: relations inside a connected system under higher-order relations (cause, implies) are kept, isolated ones are not. The rules use only the syntax of the representation, not domain content.
numbers: Mapping rules: (1) discard attributes of objects, (2) try to keep relations between objects, (3) choose systems of relations by higher-order links. Rutherford example: MORE-MASSIVE-THAN(sun,planet) maps; HOTTER-THAN(sun,planet) does not, because only mass belongs to the central-force system.
quote: A predicate that belongs to a mappable system of mutually interconnecting relationships is more likely to be imported into the target than is an isolated predicate.
limits: Theory paper with a qualitative argument and no large experiment. Assumes predicates match as identical; the text says similar-but-not-identical matching causes an infinite regress.
agent_relevance: This is the spec for O7: map relations, not surface traits, and prefer the deepest connected system. A mapping step should rank candidate matches by depth of connected structure, not by count of shared words.

source: Gentner (1983) - taxonomy of domain comparisons
finding: Comparisons differ by what overlaps. Relations only is analogy. Relations and attributes is literal similarity. Attributes only is mere appearance. Neither is an anomaly. Abstraction is analogy where the base objects are variables.
numbers: Table 1 of the paper counts attributes mapped and relations mapped per type (analogy: few attributes, many relations; mere appearance: many attributes, few relations). Water/heat example: the deep chain is CAUSE{AND[PUNCTURE, CONTAIN], FLOW-FROM}; the shallow chain is the lid/contain fact. Systematicity picks the deep chain.
limits: Qualitative scheme. Later work (Forbus 2017) dropped separate rule sets in favour of one similarity rule set in which structure wins by scoring.
agent_relevance: Gives O7 a cheap check: classify the match (relational, surface-only, both) before using an analogue. Surface-only matches should not be a source of inferences.

source: Gentner (1983) - empirical support cited in the paper (cigarette is like a time bomb)
finding: Early evidence: people who wrote interpretations of analogies such as 'A cigarette is like a time bomb' gave mostly relational content, and analogies with more relational content were rated more apt.
numbers: Reported from Gentner 1980b; no N or r is given in the 1983 paper. Fuller numbers are in Gentner and Clement 1988 (see a10).
limits: Brief description only; the numbers are in the later chapter.
agent_relevance: Supports ranking analogies by relational content, not feature overlap, when judging whether a source is apt.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: Algorithm and Examples, Artificial Intelligence 41:1-63
finding: SME is the program form of the theory. Input: two descriptions (base, target) as predicate-calculus items. Output: several global mappings (gmaps), each with correspondences, candidate inferences and a structural evaluation score (SES). It uses only structure, no domain knowledge.
numbers: Four steps: (1) local match hypotheses from match-constructor rules, (2) gmap construction by merging structurally consistent sets, (3) candidate inferences, (4) scoring. Two constraints define a gmap: one-to-one, and support (if a match is kept, matches for all its arguments are kept). The paper says SME had been applied to over 40 analogies.
limits: Needs hand-coded input representations (the later criticism). The authors say they had not done a sensitivity analysis of the weights.
agent_relevance: This is the algorithm O7 needs. The agent can write both situations as typed relation lists and let code do the matching, so the mapping is checked by a program, not by the model's say-so.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) - scoring: evidence rules and the trickle-down of systematicity
finding: Systematicity is built into the score by passing belief from a relation match down to the matches of its arguments. A match with a large structure above it gets a high score, and so do the entity pairs inside that structure.
numbers: Same-functor match gets 0.5 evidence; a rule passes 80 percent of a match's belief to its children. Gmap SES is the sum of match evidence. Dempster combination was dropped because of round-off errors with many hypotheses and because normalising stops comparison of matches across different bases.
limits: Weights are hand-set; the authors say rankings were not overly sensitive in preliminary exploration but give no numbers.
agent_relevance: A simple score the agent can compute: sum over matched items with a depth bonus. Do not normalise scores across candidate analogues if you want to compare different sources.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) - water flow to heat flow and Rutherford atom worked examples
finding: SME picks the textbook interpretation by structure alone. Heat/water: beaker to coffee, vial to ice cube, water to heat, pipe to bar, pressure to temperature, with the candidate inference that the temperature difference causes heat flow. Atom: nucleus to sun, electron to planet.
numbers: Heat/water gmaps scored 5.99, 3.94 and 2.44. Solar system/atom gmaps scored 6.03 (mass difference plus attraction, the standard reading), 4.04 (temperature mapped to mass, little supporting structure) and 1.87 (sun mass to electron mass, spurious). Run time on a Symbolics 3640: 0.70 s for water/heat (14 hypotheses), 0.91 s for solar/atom (16), 9.68 s for the larger PHINEAS case (69).
limits: Toy descriptions of 11 to 40 expressions written by the authors; the right answer is the one the authors expected.
agent_relevance: Shows the behaviour wanted from a mapping checker: several competing mappings are produced and ranked, and the spurious one scores far lower.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) - complexity analysis
finding: Most steps are polynomial, typically bounded by O(N^2) in the number of items. The merge steps can blow up: step 4(b) is O(N!) in the worst case and 4(c) can need real work, but the authors saw near best-case behaviour in practice.
numbers: Best case: one root, one gmap, constant-time merges. Worst case needs all partial gmaps to hit the same base structure in every combination.
limits: Exhaustive gmap enumeration was later replaced by greedy merge (see a19).
agent_relevance: For long scaffold runs, keep the mapper greedy and the descriptions small (tens of items) or time will grow fast.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) - simulation of a human story study (Karla the hawk)
finding: SME in analogy mode ranks the true analogy above the surface-only story; in mere-appearance mode it ranks the surface story above the true analogy. The first mirrors human soundness ratings, the second mirrors human retrieval. SME was used as a bookkeeper, not a full retrieval model.
numbers: Story set 5 (Karla vs Zerdia the country, a true analogy): analogy rules weight 22.36, appearance rules 6.41. Vs Zerdia the eagle (surface match): analogy rules 16.82, appearance rules 7.70. Five triads (15 stories) were encoded in all.
limits: One triad is worked out in the text. The human data are from Rattermann and Gentner (1987), given only in outline. Hand-encoded stories.
agent_relevance: One scorer with different match rules can model both 'is this a sound analogy' and 'what will I be reminded of'. Retrieval by surface; judgement by structure (see a17).

source: Gentner and Toupin (1986) Systematicity and surface similarity in the development of analogy, Cognitive Science 10:277-300
finding: Children acted out a story with toy animals, then acted it again with new characters. Object similarity (transparency) helped all children. A systematic story (explicit causal chain and moral) helped only the older children, and mostly when the object match was misleading.
numbers: N = 72 (36 aged 4-6, 36 aged 8-10). Mixed ANOVA, Age x Systematicity x Mapping: Age F(1,68)=14.93 p<.001; Systematicity F(1,68)=6.28 p<.05; Mapping F(2,136)=29.01; Systematicity x Mapping F(2,136)=3.89 p<.05. Older group: systematic better, t(34)=2.48 p<.01; younger t(34)=1.08 not significant. The gain was significant only in the hardest (cross-mapped) condition.
limits: No Age x Systematicity interaction in the overall test, so the age difference is not firmly shown. Systematic stories were longer (they had a moral). Small cells.
agent_relevance: Structure helps most when surface cues mislead. For the agent: supply the explicit causal chain of the source exactly when the surface match is poor or deceptive.

source: Gentner and Clement (1988) Evidence for relational selectivity in the interpretation of analogy and metaphor, Psychology of Learning and Motivation 22:307-358
finding: Experiment 1: interpretations of metaphors contained more relations than attributes, and metaphors judged most apt were those with the most relational interpretation. Attributional content did not predict aptness. This tests salience-imbalance theory (Ortony), which predicts differently.
numbers: 16 metaphors. Aptness correlated with relationality r = .65 (p<.01, judges' ratings) and r = .56 (p<.05, undergraduate ratings); with attributionality r = -.31 (not significant).
limits: Small item set (16). Relational content was rated afterwards by judges. Property-attribution accounts (Glucksberg, Ortony) fit some metaphors, and the authors accept that attribute metaphors exist.
agent_relevance: When judging whether an analogy is apt, count relational content. Surface attributes carry little weight.

source: Clement and Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping, Cognitive Science 15:89-132, Experiment 1
finding: Given two matching facts, one inside a larger shared causal system and one isolated, people say the embedded fact is the better part of the analogy. A control group who read only the target did not rate it more important.
numbers: N = 48 undergraduates, 4 passage pairs. Rating: shared-system key fact M = 6.28 vs different-system fact 4.89 (analogy group); target-only group 5.22 vs 5.31. Choice: analogy group chose the shared-system fact on average 3.17 of 4 times vs 2.0 for target-only, F(1,44)=18.43 p<.001. Per passage, analogy group 67 to 92 percent vs target-only 42 to 54 percent; Fisher exact test significant for 3 of 4 passages.
limits: Written passages about invented creatures (Tams, Robots). One passage behaved oddly and the paper links this to poor memory of that base passage (42 percent on its test).
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for systematicity as a selector: when two bits of the source could map, take the one tied into the shared causal system.

source: Clement and Gentner (1991) - Experiments 2 and 3: analogical predictions
finding: Asked to predict something about the target from the base, people mostly predicted the fact that followed from the shared causal system, not an equally plausible fact from outside it. Target-only controls mostly predicted neither.
numbers: Experiment 2: N = 32 (16 analogy, 16 target-only). Free prediction: shared-system fact .53 of analogy-group responses, different-system .12; target-only .12 and .12 (74 percent other). Choice among supplied predictions: analogy group chose the shared-system fact 87 and 69 percent on the two passages that differed significantly, target-only 44 and 25 percent. Interrater agreement .88. Experiment 3 repeated the design with a second set of materials (tables not read cell by cell).
limits: Choice differences were significant on only 2 of 4 passages in Exp 2. Short invented stories. Predictions scored by two judges.
agent_relevance: Candidate inferences should come from the part of the source that connects to matched structure. Inferences from unconnected source facts are weaker bets.

source: Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness, Cognitive Psychology 25:524-575, Experiment 1
finding: Two measures split. Soundness ratings follow shared higher-order relational structure. Retrieval from memory follows surface similarity. The two orders were uncorrelated.
numbers: N = 30 (MIT). Soundness: analogy M = 4.40, surface match 2.80, first-order-relations match 2.74; F(2,58)=70.51 p<.0001. Retrieval after 6 to 8 days (proportion of stories recalled): surface .78, analogy .44, first-order .25; F(2,58)=75.45 p<.0001. Soundness vs retrieval r(52) = .15, not significant.
limits: Stories, single lab, one-week delay. The soundness instructions were revised for Experiment 2 because of a concern that raters judged usefulness.
agent_relevance: The agent cannot count on 'remembering' the right analogue by similarity. It has to be given or searched for by structure, then checked by a structural score. Surface retrieval will favour wrong sources.

source: Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus (1993) - Experiment 2 replication of the retrieval order, as summarised in the MAC/FAC paper
finding: Experiment 2 replicated and extended Experiment 1 with a literal-similarity condition and controls, and the same retrievability order held.
numbers: Four similarity types within subjects (literal similarity, surface, analogy, first-order). MAC/FAC paper reports: 32 stories to remember, 20 probes; recall about .53 surface, .12 analogy, .03 first-order (the literal-similarity value was garbled in the PDF text); order LS >= SF > AN >= FOR stable across three variations of the study.
limits: Second-hand: the numbers were read from the MAC/FAC paper, not from the Experiment 2 tables.
agent_relevance: True analogies are rarely retrieved even by people (about 1 in 8 here). A scaffold waiting for an analogue to be recalled will mostly get surface matches.

source: Markman and Gentner (1993) Structural alignment during similarity comparisons, Cognitive Psychology 25:431-467
finding: Rating similarity first pushes people to map by relations. In a one-shot mapping task with a cross-mapped object (looks like one object but plays another's role), people who rated similarity first gave more relational mappings than people who mapped straight away.
numbers: Exp 1: relational responses .69 after similarity rating vs .42 for one-shot mapping alone (F(1,33)=7.30 p<.05); 3-mapping control .60. Exp 1b: .69 vs .47 (one-shot) vs .39 (artistry rating first), F(1,69)=6.00 and 11.44. Exp 2: high-systematicity pairs .61 vs .14 (t(22)=3.46 p<.01); low-systematicity pairs gave no clean effect, which the authors call surprising.
limits: Low-systematicity result went the unexpected way. Picture stimuli with deliberately misleading object matches. Item analysis (6 of 8 pairs) was not significant by sign test. Four experiments in all; Exp 3 and 4 not summarised here.
agent_relevance: Asking for an explicit comparison pulls people to the relational match. A mapping prompt that asks for a full comparison before the answer may push an LLM the same way (untested).

source: Markman and Gentner (1993) - SME simulation of the cross-mapping experiment
finding: In literal-similarity mode SME produces both an object-based and a relation-based interpretation and prefers the relation-based one when the matching structure is deep. The object match wins only if its score gets higher, by adding shared attributes or shrinking the matching relational structure.
numbers: The top relation-based gmap scored 12.94 in the Experiment 1 simulation. Score rises with the depth of matching relations and the number of shared attributes on paired objects.
limits: One simulated item pair; no fit statistic against the human data.
agent_relevance: A concrete rule for when to trust a surface match: only when relational support is thin. The mapper can report the score gap between the best relational and the best object mapping.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Law (1995) MAC/FAC: a model of similarity-based retrieval, Cognitive Science 19:141-205
finding: Retrieval in two stages. MAC: a cheap dot product over content vectors (counts of predicates) picks a few candidates by surface-heavy overlap. FAC: SME scores the survivors structurally. This reproduces the human order LS >= surface > analogy >= first-order.
numbers: Simulation on 9 story sets (45 stories). Thagard's ARCS on the Karla story with 100 fable distractors gave activations LS .67, FOR -.11, SF -.17, AN -.27, which breaks the human order twice. MAC/FAC ran about two orders of magnitude faster than ARCS on identical data. ARCS did not settle after 1,000 iterations on some inputs (runs up to 12 hours).
limits: Matches the ordering, not item-level human data. The ARCS comparison uses the SME authors' encodings.
agent_relevance: A two-stage design for analogue search: fast shallow filter, then a structural score on a handful. Fits our need for cheap retrieval plus a checked mapping.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Lovett, Gentner (2017) Extending SME to handle large-scale cognitive modeling, Cognitive Science 41:1152-1201 - what changed since 1989
finding: Five changes: greedy merge (one to three best mappings in O(n^2 log n)), incremental mapping, ubiquitous predicates (relations like 'cause' that should not drive alignment), structural evaluation of candidate inferences, and match filters for task constraints. Analogy and similarity now share one rule set; structure wins through the scoring.
numbers: Defaults: at most 3 mappings; keep only mappings within 20 percent of the best score (cutoff 0.8). Over 5,843 mapping runs from five task models, run time tracks n^2 log n at R^2 > 0.9 for geometric analogies, oddity task, thermodynamics and AP physics, and R^2 > 0.36 for moral decision-making. Actual match hypotheses were 2 to 32 percent of the worst case on average.
limits: Greedy merge may miss the exhaustive optimum. Description size still drives cost.
agent_relevance: A tested design for a code-based mapper: greedy, at most 3 candidate mappings, a score cutoff, and inference scoring. Safe to run inside the scaffold at the sizes our typed lists will have.

source: Forbus and Oblinger (1990) greedy merge, as reported in Forbus et al. (2017)
finding: A simple greedy merge found the same best mapping as exhaustive merge in most of 56 test analogies.
numbers: Identical best mapping in 52 of 56 analogies (93 percent). Grootswagers (2013), reported in the same paper: greedy matched exhaustive in 87.5 percent of generated pairs and 99.89 percent of pairs of plays from the ACME datasets.
limits: Second-hand via the 2017 paper. The 56 analogies came from SME's own example library, and Grootswagers measured score optimality rather than identity, a different criterion.
agent_relevance: Greedy mapping is nearly as good as exhaustive and far cheaper, so the scaffold needs no exhaustive search over mappings.

source: Wolff and Gentner (2011) Structure-mapping in metaphor comprehension, as reported in Forbus et al. (2017) and Gentner and Forbus (2025)
finding: Under a very short deadline people judge a directional metaphor and its reverse equally comprehensible. By about 1,200 to 1,600 ms they prefer the forward one. This supports an early symmetric alignment and a later directional projection of inferences, as SME does.
numbers: Deadlines of 500 or 600 ms (no forward/reverse difference; scrambled and literal items still separated), 1,200 ms and 1,600 ms (clear forward advantage), as given in the two reviews.
limits: Second-hand; the original sample sizes were not read. One lab.
agent_relevance: Supports a two-phase design: align first, then project inferences in one direction. O7 can do the same: map, then choose the direction of inference.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Everett, Wu (1997) Towards a computational model of evaluating and using analogical inferences, CogSci 19:229-234
finding: Adds a score for candidate inferences. Support: how much of the inference rests on the mapping. Extrapolation: how far it goes beyond the mapping. Candidate inferences are held as defeasible beliefs justified by the mapping and retracted if a contradiction appears. The same score reproduces several induction findings.
numbers: A simulation of Lassaline (1996): adding a base relation that explains the inferred property raises inductive strength, and the model reproduces this with the inference support score. Heit and Rubenstein (1994) and Osherson et al. (1990) orderings are reproduced in qualitative form.
limits: Proposal paper with worked examples, not a large fit to data. The support and extrapolation formulas were first-pass.
agent_relevance: Two numbers for any transferred step: how much of it is supported by matched structure, and how far it extrapolates. Low support plus high extrapolation means test it before use. Keeps inferences retractable.

source: Lovett and Forbus (2017) Modeling visual problem solving as analogical reasoning, Psychological Review 124:60-90
finding: A model of Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices built on SME (with CogSketch for perception) solved 56 of 60 problems, above the average of the college students tested. Human item difficulty was predicted by whether the model needed re-representation.
numbers: Model 56/60, 75th percentile of 1993 US adult norms. Human sample: 42 Northwestern students (2 excluded), 36 3x3 items, mean 30.0/36, equal to 54/60 and the 61st percentile. Regressions of item accuracy on model factors explained .63 and .67 of variance. The four model failures (D11, D12, E11, E12) were among the hardest for people.
limits: Hand-built symbolic inputs from sketches; the stimuli were recreated by the authors. The model does not predict the wrong answers people choose.
agent_relevance: SME-style comparison with strategy shifts can solve an abstract-reasoning test. A warning too: the gain came from careful representation and re-representation, not from the matcher alone.

source: Gentner and Forbus (2025) The Structure-Mapping Engine: a multidecade interaction between psychology and artificial intelligence, Current Directions in Psychological Science
finding: Latest summary by the two authors. SME works in three stages (local matches, structurally consistent kernels, merged mappings with inferences and a score). Graph matching is NP-complete in general and SME uses an efficient approximate merge, O(n^2 log n). They call it an open question whether generative AI can do analogical processing without a symbol system.
numbers: CogSketch with SME scores at the 61st percentile on Raven's. Other models named: LISA, DORA, IAM, SIAM, ACME, Copycat. Analogical learning is described as incremental, more data-efficient than deep learning, and inspectable.
quote: whether generative AI systems are capable of doing analogical processing without hybridization with a symbol system remains an open question
limits: Review by the authors of SME. No direct LLM comparison is run. Use of vector embeddings inside SME (Liang et al. 2016) is mentioned as an early hybrid.
agent_relevance: Confirms no tested LLM plus SME pairing as of this paper, and names the hybrid (LLM writes structure, symbolic engine maps) as an open direction.

source: ACME (Holyoak and Thagard 1989) and ARCS (Thagard et al. 1990) as described in the MAC/FAC paper
finding: ACME is the main constraint-satisfaction rival. It builds a network like SME's match hypotheses and settles to one interpretation using structural, semantic and pragmatic constraints. ARCS is its retrieval version.
numbers: In the MAC/FAC study both ARCS and MAC/FAC retrieved Sour Grapes from a fables memory, but MAC/FAC was about two orders of magnitude faster. ARCS showed a possible bias toward larger descriptions when 25 plays were added to memory.
limits: Comparison run by the SME authors, not the ACME authors. ACME itself was not read.
agent_relevance: Alternative engines exist, but the structural family agrees on the constraints (one-to-one, parallel connectivity, systematicity). The choice of engine matters less than the representation.

source: Turney (2008) The Latent Relation Mapping Engine: algorithm and experiments, JAIR 33:615-655
finding: Removes SME's hand-coded input. Given only two word lists (base terms, target terms), it scores relations between words using corpus statistics and finds the best one-to-one mapping.
numbers: Accuracy 91.5 percent on 20 mapping problems vs a human average of 87.6 percent (difference not significant, paired t-test). Best alternative 76.8 percent. Latent Relational Analysis, the relation scorer, got 56 percent on 374 SAT analogy questions vs an average human 57 percent; attributional similarity best 35 percent.
limits: Word-level analogies; 20 problems of about 7 items. No systematicity or candidate inferences; entity correspondence only.
agent_relevance: A cheap automatic route to entity correspondences when hand-coded relations are not affordable. Today an LLM could replace the corpus statistics.

source: Jacob, Shani, Shahaf (2023) FAME: Flexible, Scalable Analogy Mappings Engine, arXiv 2311.01860
finding: A descendant of SME for word-level domain pairs. It builds the relations from commonsense sources and a language model (GPT-3.5), then maps. It beat the Latent Relation Mapping Engine and a human baseline on its test sets.
numbers: 2x2 classical problems: 81.2 percent mapped (chance 50). Larger problems: 77.8 percent perfect mappings (chance 13.1). On 80 problems from Green et al. (2010): near analogies 85 percent, far 77.5 percent. Against humans on one task: 90 percent vs 70.2 percent.
limits: Maps entity lists, not full systematic structures; no candidate-inference scoring. Test sets are small. The knowledge source mattered: its ablation tables show different sources giving different scores.
agent_relevance: An existing pattern of LLM feeding a mapper. The quality of the generated relations decides the result.

source: Khojasteh et al. (2026) YARN: enhancing structural mapping with LLM-derived abstractions for analogical reasoning in narratives, arXiv 2603.29997
finding: An LLM splits stories into units and abstracts them; a structural mapper then aligns the units. Without abstraction the mapper is below chance; with abstraction it beats LLM-only on a multiple-choice set and on far narrative analogies, but loses on near ones.
numbers: Mapping without abstraction (Qwen): 0.17 on the multiple-choice set (chance 0.25) and 0.24 on far ARN analogies (chance 0.50). With conceptual plus evaluative abstraction: 0.46 (Qwen, vs best LLM-only 0.41) and 0.45 (Llama, vs 0.28 LLM-only). ARN near analogies: chain-of-thought 0.79 vs YARN 0.69 for Qwen; far: zero-shot 0.52 vs YARN 0.47 (Qwen); Llama far 0.46 vs 0.42 for LLM-only.
limits: The mapper compares units by embedding cosine similarity, not SME's predicate rules; SME is cited as the model. Small open-weight models, two datasets. Several ARN far cells stay below the 0.50 random baseline.
agent_relevance: Mapping raw text fails; abstracting units to roles is the step that matters. Matches the schema stance: typed relations first, then code does the mapping.

source: Donvito and Lieto (2026) Structural ranking of the cognitive plausibility of computational models of analogy and metaphors with the Minimal Cognitive Grid, arXiv 2605.01359
finding: A formal comparison of SME, CogSketch, METCL and LLMs on whether they implement the constraints of structure-mapping theory. SME and CogSketch score highest on structure and match to human data; LLMs score highest on generality and lowest on structural fit.
numbers: Functional/structural ratio: SME and CogSketch 0.606, METCL 0.407, LLMs 0.109. Generality: LLMs 0.500, CogSketch 0.125, SME 0.063. Performance match: SME and CogSketch 0.923, METCL 0.714, LLMs 0.578. Composite plausibility, two weighting schemes: CogSketch 0.576 or 0.551, SME 0.543 or 0.531, METCL 0.440 or 0.415, LLMs 0.496 or 0.396 (the paper's two weighting schemes; which is which was not checked).
limits: Scores come from the authors' own grid and the literature, not a new experiment. LLM evidence is from GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and GPT-4o; none for newer systems.
agent_relevance: LLMs show no built-in one-to-one or parallel-connectivity bias, so the scaffold should enforce them in code.

source: Gentner and Markman (1993) Analogy: watershed or Waterloo? Structural alignment and the development of connectionist models of analogy, NIPS 5:855-862
finding: Argues that any model of cognition, symbolic or subsymbolic, has to capture structural alignment: comparing relational representations, projecting structure from one case to the other, and flexibility. It uses this as a test for neural network models of analogy.
numbers: No new numbers; a summary of the psychological phenomena that connectionist models must reproduce.
limits: Position paper by the SME camp.
agent_relevance: The challenge applies to LLMs as distributed models; the scaffold answers it by putting binding and one-to-one checks in code.

source: Gentner and Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity, American Psychologist 52:45-56, benchmark phenomena as listed in Forbus et al. (2017) Table 1
finding: Similarity and analogy are one process, structural alignment. Benchmark phenomena any model should reproduce: relational similarity, structural consistency (one-to-one and parallel connectivity), systematicity, candidate inferences, alignable differences, interactive interpretation, multiple interpretations, cross-mapping.
numbers: Listed in Table 1 of the 2017 paper, adapted from Markman and Gentner (2000).
limits: Second-hand list. Rivals (Holyoak and Thagard, Hummel and Holyoak, Hofstadter) disagree on how semantics and pragmatics enter.
agent_relevance: A checklist for testing the mapper in the scaffold: one-to-one, parallel connectivity, systematic preference, alignable-difference reporting.
